What Is DNS? How Does a Domain Name Lead to an IP Address?

When you enter https://www.example.com, the browser needs an address to connect to before it can request the page. The URL gives it the name www.example.com. The browser uses DNS (Domain Name System) to look up the IP address for that name.

Think of tapping someone's name in your phone contacts. The phone looks up the saved number and calls it. The domain name is like the person's name, the IP address is like the number, and DNS is like the contacts list. In practice, many DNS servers share responsibility for the records.

What Is an IP Address?

Computers, phones, and servers use numeric IP addresses to communicate over a network. Like a phone number on a call, an IP address helps identify where to send data. There are two formats you will encounter.

FormatExampleWhat it looks like
IPv4192.0.2.10Four groups of decimal digits separated by dots.
IPv62001:db8::10Groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons. IPv6 supports more addresses than IPv4.

A laptop connected to home Wi-Fi might have a private IP address such as 192.168.1.10. It uses that address on the home network. When you open a website over the internet, the browser may connect to the public IP address of a web server, a load balancer that distributes requests, or a content delivery network (CDN).

A domain name can resolve to several IP addresses. Several websites can also share one IP address. If moving to a new host changes the address, you can update the DNS records and keep the domain name.

How Is a Domain Name Structured?

Read www.example.com from right to left to see how the parts fit together.

PartWhat it means
.comA top-level domain (TLD). .org, .net, and .mm are other examples.
example.comThe registered domain name in this example. example is the name under .com.
www.example.comA subdomain of example.com. Another possible subdomain is blog.example.com.

To use your own domain name, register an available name through a domain registrar and renew the registration to keep using it after its term ends. Once you have a name, you need hosting to make the website available at that name.

What Does Web Hosting Do?

Web hosting makes a website available over the internet. A basic site can include HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images. A web app can also run a backend that receives requests and generates responses. If the app needs a database, it can connect to a separate database service.

A web server is software that accepts HTTP requests from the browser and sends responses. It can run on a physical server, a virtual machine, or infrastructure managed by a hosting provider.

Hosting typeHow it works
Shared hostingSeveral websites share resources such as CPU and memory on a server.
VPSYou can install and manage software on a virtual machine allocated to you.
Dedicated serverYou get a physical server for your own use.
Managed hostingYou deploy the website and the provider manages the infrastructure. Vercel and Firebase Hosting are examples.

After deployment, the hosting provider may give you an IP address or a hostname. Add the value supplied by the provider to the DNS record so visitors can open the site at www.example.com.

How Does the Browser Look Up www.example.com?

The browser or operating system can check whether it still has a cached DNS answer. If there is no usable answer, it asks a recursive resolver. Your network may provide one, or you can use a public resolver such as Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) or Google Public DNS (8.8.8.8).

If the resolver has neither the answer nor the relevant referrals cached, it follows these steps.

  1. The root nameserver directs the resolver to the TLD nameservers responsible for .com.
  2. The .com TLD nameserver directs it to the authoritative nameservers responsible for the example.com DNS records.
  3. The authoritative nameserver returns the record for www.example.com. The record can contain an IP address or another hostname that the resolver needs to look up.

The resolver handles these queries and returns the resulting IP address. The browser connects to that address and, once the HTTPS connection is established, requests the page from the web server.

What Does a DNS Record Specify?

In the hosting example above, use an A record when the provider supplies an IPv4 address. If the provider supplies a hostname for www to point to, a CNAME record is commonly used.

RecordWhat it doesExample
AMaps a name to an IPv4 address.example.com → 192.0.2.10
AAAAMaps a name to an IPv6 address.example.com → 2001:db8::10
CNAMEMakes a name an alias for another hostname. The resolver continues the lookup using that hostname.www.example.com → example.com
MXSpecifies the mail server that receives email for the domain.example.com → mail.example.com

In the CNAME example, the browser keeps using www.example.com while the resolver looks up the IP address for example.com. An HTTP redirect that changes the address in the browser is configured on the web server side.

Try nslookup on Windows

Run these commands one at a time in Command Prompt.

nslookup -type=A example.com
nslookup -type=A example.com 1.1.1.1
nslookup -type=A example.com 8.8.8.8

-type=A requests the A record, which contains an IPv4 address. The first command queries your device's configured resolver. The other two commands query the resolver specified at the end of the command, so you can try them without changing your device's DNS settings.

Server and Address at the top of the output show the resolver you queried. Look below for the IPv4 address returned for example.com. Replace -type=A with -type=AAAA to look for IPv6 addresses.
